title: Machine Learning Based Detection of Previously Unseen Low Rate DDoS Attacks
items: Extended Literature Review and Research Methodology Development

We propose a reproducible evaluation of whether a compact machine-learning intrusion detection system can recognize previously unseen slow denial-of-service behaviour while maintaining a low false-positive rate on ordinary and stressed legitimate traffic. The candidate detector combines supervised learning on known attacks with an autoencoder trained on benign observations. Its contribution is a controlled evaluation of attack novelty, low-rate behaviour, benign stress and detection delay together; superior performance is a hypothesis to test.

Eight additional research articles from 2025-2026 extend the three Phase 1 papers. The extended review refines the original gap because recent studies already provide hybrid detectors and strict zero-day holdouts. The proposed work concentrates on the remaining operating tradeoff and the quality of the evidence used to measure it.

The project remains limited to detection and evaluation. Its output is a timestamped alert with supporting scores. Automatic blocking, rate limiting, traffic redirection and mitigation-effectiveness experiments are outside the implementation scope.

title: Deliverable 1 Extended literature review
items: The search covered publisher article pages and accessible author manuscripts using combinations of low-rate DDoS, slow DoS, zero-day intrusion detection, autoencoder, temporal detection, false positives and lightweight classification. Inclusion required an original 2025-2026 research article, a Q1-Q2 venue under the stated ranking system, and identifiable data, method and evaluation. Surveys, editorials, duplicate records and papers without usable experimental information were excluded. This is a focused critical review rather than a claimed exhaustive systematic review.

The eight additions A1-A8 below are distinct from the Phase 1 studies by Bocu and Iavich [1], Rullo et al. [2] and Nakip [3]. A4 and A7 contribute directly relevant DDoS classifier baselines and evaluation lessons; they are not treated as evidence that unseen low-rate attacks have been solved. Dataset documentation is supporting material and is not counted toward the eight articles.

title: Critical analysis of additional papers A1 to A4
items: F-OSFA: A Fog Level Generalizable Solution for Zero-Day DDOS Attacks Detection

F-OSFA proposes a CNN/decision-tree classifier, a benign-trained contractive autoencoder and a resource-use analyser. Its abstract reports zero-day accuracies of 96.77% on CIC-DDoS2019 and 95.98% on CIC-IDS2017. However, its future-work section still calls for a resource-labelled dataset to implement the resource analyser, so those headline results do not establish validation of every proposed component. The abstract's few-shot terminology also differs from the methodology's zero-shot module. Hybrid detection is therefore established, while unseen slow-family recall at a fixed benign-stress false-positive budget remains a distinct evaluation question [4].
Hybrid dual-head IDS: A lightweight and explainable deep learning DDOS/DOS framework for zero-day and imbalanced attack detection in IoT networks

The dual-head framework combines supervised classification with anomaly detection, uses dataset-adaptive minority augmentation including WGAN-GP, and supplies SHAP explanations. CIC-IoT2023, BoT-IoT and ToN-IoT experiments include a true zero-day holdout, component ablations and five-seed validation. The paper reports accuracy and F1 above 99.5% across its evaluated datasets and approximately 0.5 MB model size. Therefore, a claim that recent IDS research lacks strict holdouts is no longer defensible. Its broad intrusion results do not establish the specific unseen slow-attack versus benign-stress tradeoff investigated here. Reported per-sample inference cost also cannot replace attack-onset-to-alert delay [5].
Adapting Convolutional Autoencoder for DDoS Attack Detection via Joint Reconstruction Learning and Refined Anomaly Scoring

CA-CAE uses consecutive asymmetric convolutional autoencoders with joint reconstruction and a score weighted by recency and relative traffic volume. Cisco NetFlow measurements contain 190,817 normal and 78 anomalous instances; the reported F1 rises from 0.515 for the baseline CAE to 0.934. Differencing and overlapping windows make this relevant to temporal anomaly detection. However, volume weighting requires testing when an attack deliberately has low volume, and only 78 anomalies constrain uncertainty estimates. The counts imply about 0.041% anomalies, rather than the 0.0004% printed in the article. This arithmetic discrepancy should not be propagated into our experimental design [6].
Lightweight machine learning framework for efficient DDoS attack detection in IoT networks

This study compares Random Forest, Logistic Regression and Naive Bayes after cleaning, encoding, scaling and ExtraTrees selection of 18 features from NSL-KDD. It reports Random Forest accuracy of 99.88% and F1 of 99.87%, using an 80:20 split and tenfold validation. It provides a useful justification for including inexpensive classical baselines rather than assuming deep learning is necessary. The authors acknowledge that NSL-KDD is not IoT-specific and may not represent current traffic. Neither conventional cross-validation nor this dataset establishes unseen low-rate DDoS detection. We retain the baseline lesson while selecting slow-attack traces and temporally separated sessions for our own evaluation [7].

title: Critical analysis of additional papers A5 to A8
items: Federated sparse-learning framework for detecting low-rate stealth attacks in resource-constrained IoT devices

FSL-IDS targets low-rate stealth attacks through sparse local encoding, fog-level temporal correlation and cloud aggregation, with training-only synthetic stealth augmentation and quantization. The authors report IoTID20-based experiments, cloud ROC-AUC 0.992 and F1 0.965, plus substantial recall loss when augmentation is removed. This makes temporal context and component ablation relevant to our design. However, the reported stealth labels and augmented data require provenance auditing; they should not automatically be treated as native benchmark categories. Exposure to stealth samples during training also differs from excluding an entire slow-attack family. Our evaluation therefore separates attack novelty from rarity and records the origin of every label [8].
Liquid neural networks for adaptive DDoS detection in IoT and SDN environments

This work combines liquid time-constant layers and attention, independently training and evaluating on SNT-SDN2025, CICIoT2023 and IoT23. Cleaning and standardization precede ten-flow sequences; a chronological 70:30 split is made before window generation. The maximum reported accuracy is 99.96%, with 0.07% FPR on CICIoT2023. The temporal separation is a useful leakage-control pattern. However, independently fitting a model on each dataset is not frozen-model cross-dataset transfer, and future traffic is not necessarily a new attack family. We adopt the split-before-window principle and evaluate both novelty and transfer explicitly rather than treating temporal modelling alone as evidence of either [9].
A lightweight machine learning approach for DDoS detection and classification

The paper studies compact feature subsets with Random Forest, KNN, Complement Naive Bayes and Logistic Regression on CIC-DDoS2019, using LDAP, MSSQL, UDP and benign traffic. It removes identifying metadata, cleans invalid values, encodes labels and compares NearMiss-balanced and imbalanced experiments. Table 23 reports RF accuracy 99.32% and F1 99.40%. This supports compact baselines and reporting computational cost. Its documented balancing-before-splitting workflow warrants a leakage audit, and the selected flooding classes do not certify slow-attack performance. In our pipeline, every learned transformation and any resampling occur strictly within training, while test prevalence is preserved [10].
Dynamic graph neural network-based framework to increase detection accuracy in SDN under DDOS

GCTNetwork integrates gated temporal graph layers, edge-aware LSTM and graph attention on an SDN testbed-derived flow dataset. It applies log transforms, min-max scaling and graph construction, reporting 94.08% accuracy and 93.27% F1 against ST-GCN, GRAN and LR-STGCN. Graph context is relevant to coordinated activity that individual flows may hide. However, the presented classes are benign and ICMP/TCP/UDP floods, rather than a dedicated unseen slow-family evaluation. The training configuration states ten epochs while the learning-curve discussion describes 100, creating a reproducibility ambiguity. Our simpler aggregation retains temporal context with explicit settings and matched comparisons [11].

title: Methodological synthesis across the literature
items: The review identifies four established approaches: classical supervised flow classification; benign-trained reconstruction or one-class detection; hybrid known-attack and anomaly branches; and temporal or graph modelling of coordinated behaviour. Feature cleaning, reduced representations and thresholded scores recur, but they address different experimental questions. A random or stratified split measures recognition within a sampled distribution; a time split measures later traffic; a family holdout measures attack novelty; and frozen transfer measures change of environment. These should be reported separately [4-11].
Design choices supported by the review

Use a modest hybrid as a testable candidate; locate the contribution in the evaluation problem
Temporal representations can expose subtle activity [6,8,9,11]
Use fixed-time destination aggregates and strictly causal rolling features
Include Logistic Regression and Random Forest alongside the proposed method
Reconstruction and augmentation choices influence performance [5,6,8]
Measure the effect of each branch and temporal component; avoid synthetic attack augmentation in the core study
Published metrics use different datasets and units [4-11]
Do not rank papers by their headline accuracy; compare our implementations on identical splits

items: The earlier broad gap about an absence of strict unseen-attack protocols must be narrowed: A2 explicitly includes such a protocol [5]. Our central question becomes whether unseen slow attacks can be detected at a threshold fixed before testing while legitimate bursts and congestion remain below an acceptable false-alarm level. The study also asks what temporal observation costs are required to obtain that performance.

The following comparison tables use the assignment fields for all eight additions. Results are attached to their original tasks and datasets. FAI means false alarm index; ZDS means zero-day separation; AE means autoencoder; LRSA means low-rate stealth attack; DR means detection rate. Limitations are our critical interpretations unless explicitly attributed to the authors.

title: Deliverable 2 Refined research gap
items: Existing work already demonstrates high benchmark accuracy, benign-trained anomaly detection, hybrids, temporal representations and strict holdouts. The narrower opportunity is to measure their joint reliability when an excluded slow-attack family and unusual legitimate traffic are both encountered after thresholds are frozen. The table triangulates four potential gaps using three especially relevant additions; it does not claim that every prior paper omits every experiment.

rows: G1 Joint novelty and benign stress
Test an excluded slow family and reserved benign-stress sessions at the same frozen threshold
Separate observation wait, feature cost and inference from onset-to-alert delay
Publish a label map and split manifest; perform frozen external testing on compatible features
Three proposed prongs; resource validation limited
Compare a compact hybrid with simple baselines and isolate component gains

items: Within the reviewed studies, evidence remains insufficient to establish whether a compact, reproducible detector can maintain useful recall on a completely excluded slow-attack family while respecting a threshold calibrated to at most 1% false positives on development benign traffic, and how that operating point changes under reserved benign stress and network transfer. This is an evaluation and generalization gap, not a claim of inventing hybrid detection or the first zero-day protocol.
Why it matters and how the study addresses it

An IDS that reacts to every legitimate burst can generate an impractical number of alerts; a detector that waits for a completed long connection may recognize a slow attack too late. We will hold out complete families, fit all preprocessing only on training, calibrate on separate benign sessions, freeze the full pipeline, and report per-family recall, stress FPR and onset-to-alert delay. Negative findings will identify the boundary of the method rather than be hidden by average accuracy.

title: Research questions objectives and claim boundaries
items: Can a compact supervised-plus-anomaly IDS detect previously unseen slow DoS-DDoS behaviour at a low false-positive operating point, including on stressed legitimate traffic, with acceptable observation and computation delay?

Per-family and macro recall; episode recall; confusion counts

FPR, FP count and benign denominator for each workload

items: Previously unseen means the test family is absent from training, model selection, threshold calibration and attack augmentation. It does not mean an unknown software vulnerability. A time split alone is insufficient. Low-rate status must be supported by the attack mechanism and measured traffic rates; a random low-percentile sample from a flood dataset will not be relabelled as a genuine low-rate attack.

H1: the hybrid improves excluded-family recall over the supervised branch at its matched development FPR. H2: causal temporal context improves unseen slow-attack episode recall over instantaneous features. H3: persistence reduces benign-stress alerts, with a measurable delay cost. These are testable hypotheses, not assumed outcomes.

CIC-IDS2017 Slowloris and Slowhttptest support slow DoS evidence [12]. Distributed low-rate DDoS claims additionally require multiple independently logged source clients in the isolated lab. Offline CSV classification cannot establish live detection latency. Likewise, an unusual low-rate malicious trace without measured service degradation supports detection of attack attempts, not successful denial of service. Broader Internet or production IoT effectiveness will remain outside the demonstrated scope.

title: Deliverable 3 Research methodology inputs and collection
items: The primary input is timestamped packet metadata grouped by destination service into non-overlapping one-second windows. Each record retains dataset, capture, session, attack family, time, traffic-condition and label provenance for splitting and evaluation; identifiers are not predictive features. The online feature builder uses only packets already observed. Rolling context uses the preceding ten seconds, with shorter and longer histories considered on development data only.

The binary target is benign versus attack-associated activity, with original attack families retained for reporting. A positive window must contain attack packets identified by audited flow/packet labels or lab event logs; time inside a scheduled attack interval alone is insufficient. Reconcile time zones, flow direction, five-tuples and NAT mappings before joining labels. Retain ambiguous mixed windows in a separate sensitivity analysis with their counts. Episode timing follows logged attack start/end; service availability and response-time logs evaluate lab impact but are not model inputs.

items: Before modelling, build a manifest containing source URLs, downloaded file hashes, extraction version, label map, family aliases, usable sample counts and session IDs. Reconcile labels against schedules and capture metadata; retain excluded/ambiguous counts. Report the audited usable counts and final class distribution after collection.

The isolated lab uses one web service, three separate client containers or VMs, and a monitor. Benign conditions are ordinary request traffic, bursts, flash-crowd-like concurrency and controlled congestion. Use benign-only infrastructure pilots; no Slowloris/Slowhttptest examples may influence feature choice, fitting, validation or calibration. Reserve two attack mechanisms (incomplete-header and slow-request-body connection holding), one or three active clients, and two prespecified concurrency/timing profiles: 10 connections with 20-second spacing, or 60 connections with 5-second spacing per client. These are design settings, not evidence that every trace is low-rate or service-denying. Record actual rates and service impact after freezing; retain unsuccessful attempts. No external targets are contacted.

title: Methodology preprocessing and feature representation
items: Assign independent raw sessions to partitions before creating windows or fitting transformations. Quarantine all sessions containing an excluded family, including their benign context. Audit exact duplicates without labels or model scores and remove copied versions across partitions. For unavoidable contiguous-block splits, remove crossing flow intervals and purge at least the maximum candidate history plus connection-tracker timeout. Reset feature and persistence state at session boundaries; use warm-up packets only from the same partition.

Discard labels, attack filenames, source/destination IPs, absolute timestamps and raw port identifiers from model inputs. Identifiers may route aggregation and establish groups only. Map protocol to a fixed schema; standardize units, directional definitions and byte/packet counting. Replace impossible infinities with missing values, impute using branch-specific training medians (benign-only for the AE), and keep missing-value indicators. Do not discard unusual but valid observations merely because they are outliers.

For the AE, apply log1p to predefined non-negative heavy-tailed counts and durations, then robust centring/scaling learned from training benign data only. Apply the frozen mapping to all later data. The supervised branch uses the same feature definitions; it may consume the unscaled numeric values through its own fitted preprocessing. Fit constant-column removal within the corresponding branch's training data too. The core study uses class weights, not attack synthesis or test-set balancing.

items: Use incremental, as-of-time counters. A completed-flow duration or total bytes from the future must never appear in an earlier decision. In PCAP experiments, re-extract the same window schema for each source. If only finished-flow CSVs are feasible, run a separately labelled offline analysis and omit claims about early/live detection delay. Fix the feature list and history length using development data; the main no-temporal ablation removes only rolling history, leaving instantaneous inputs intact.

title: Methodology proposed detector and baselines
items: Step 5 Proposed model and decision rule

Use HistGradientBoosting (HGB) on benign and permitted known attacks with inverse-frequency sample weights. Disable its internal random early-stopping split; select boosting iterations on grouped development V within the stated tuning budget. The anomaly branch is a dense AE fitted only to benign training windows, initially d-32-16-8-16-32-d with ReLU hidden layers and linear reconstruction. Minimize mean squared error with Adam, initially learning rate 0.001 and batch size 256; use benign V for early stopping, a 100-epoch cap and patience ten. The input dimension d follows the frozen feature schema. These are proposed CPU-oriented settings, not measured findings.

Let pS(x) be the supervised attack score and r(x) the AE mean reconstruction error. Convert each to a benign-tail percentile using a disjoint benign score-reference set C1: uS(x) = ECDF_C1(pS(x)) and uA(x) = ECDF_C1(r(x)). The hybrid score is s(x) = max(uS(x), uA(x)). This is a calibrated ranking score, not a probability that the attack is zero-day. An alert occurs when at least k of the last m window scores for a destination exceed threshold t. Candidate persistence rules are 1-of-1, 2-of-3 and 3-of-5.

Use a separate benign set C2, including ordinary and development-stress sessions, to calibrate the complete threshold-plus-persistence rule. For each candidate, require empirical C2 FPR <=1% both overall and within each of the ordinary/stress strata; report denominators and uncertainty. Branch-wise 1% allowances do not imply a 1% OR-rule FPR. Among feasible candidates select the best known-attack V episode recall, breaking ties by lower delay then lower complexity. An always-silent rule is feasible but may be useless: if detection collapses under the constraint, report that tradeoff. Freeze all transforms, weights, C1 mappings, the threshold and persistence before final tests.

items: Use identical available features, source partitions, calibration sets and test sessions for all models. Apply the same persistence candidates and final-rule FPR calibration. Run stochastic models with seeds 7, 19, 42, 73 and 101; deterministic methods need one fitted run. Literature architectures requiring unavailable telemetry or private data serve as contextual references rather than claimed reproductions.

title: Methodology experimental design
items: Before any fitting, quarantine the whole Slowloris/Slowhttptest group, family aliases and associated complete public sessions as novelty test U. All corresponding lab attack sessions are also final-only. None may enter training, early stopping, feature selection, augmentation, C1, C2 or V. The entire external CSE-CIC-IDS2018 source, including benign records, is reserved separately. Grouping related slow variants together avoids learning a close relative. Secondary Hulk or GoldenEye exclusions test broader novelty, not additional slow-family diversity.

Allocate remaining eligible public groups and benign lab sessions approximately as 50% fitting, 15% known-attack/benign development V, 10% benign score reference C1, 10% benign calibration C2, and 15% final known/benign K. These are group-level planning proportions, not row-wise stratification: family quarantine and benign-only C1/C2 eligibility take precedence. Keep final lab-stress sessions separate. If independent public sessions are scarce, use purged contiguous blocks and publish exact counts and dependence limits. Every model uses the same manifest; no external-source records enter these development partitions.

items: Run at least five independent final sessions for each of the four benign conditions. For attacks, two mechanisms x two source counts x two concurrency/timing profiles x five fresh-session replicates gives 40 planned episodes. Reserve all these attack runs until the detector is frozen; development lab traffic is benign only. Reset the service and clients between runs, vary background/workload seeds, provide a benign warm-up longer than the maximum history, and observe for 180 seconds after onset or until episode end. Record packet/byte rates, active connections and service degradation; publish failed attempts and missed detections too.

Primary external transfer applies the complete model and threshold unchanged to CSE-CIC-IDS2018. Lab sessions from an environment used for benign calibration are stress/distribution tests, not evidence of unseen-environment transfer. Re-extract compatible features from PCAP where possible; otherwise omit that source with an explicit limitation. Optional target-benign recalibration is a separate adaptation experiment with its own disjoint split and cannot replace frozen transfer. Never use test outcomes to select low-rate cutoffs or configurations.

title: Methodology evaluation and statistical comparison
items: Treat attack as positive. Report confusion counts TP, FP, TN and FN, along with the total number of benign windows, attack windows and independent sessions. Primary outcomes are per-family unseen recall and ordinary/stress FPR at the frozen development-calibrated operating point. The <=1% development FPR is a design target, not a guarantee for final or transferred data.

rows: Recall = TP/(TP+FN); precision = TP/(TP+FP). Report each unseen family separately
F1 = 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN); accuracy = (TP+TN)/N. Supplementary, because prevalence can dominate
FPR = FP/(FP+TN). Show percentages, counts and normal/stress strata separately
Use average precision (AP) as the prespecified precision-recall summary under imbalance; ROC-AUC is supplementary. Keep frozen-threshold results primary
New eligible alert episodes during the attack horizon / all attack episodes; delay is first eligible alert timestamp minus logged onset
Median/p95 feature and inference time, throughput, peak memory, and merged benign alert episodes per hour

items: Separate score-computation latency from observation wait. End-to-end delay includes window closure, history warm-up when relevant, persistence and processing. An eligible detection is a newly starting alert episode after logged attack onset, within 180 seconds and before the episode ends; an alert already active before onset is not credited as immediate attack detection. New alert episodes require five preceding non-alert windows. Report pre-existing alerts, misses and censoring separately, window FPR before merging, conditional delay among detections, and detection fractions by 10/30/60/180 seconds with denominators and time at risk. Undefined precision/AUC values are N/A, not silently zero.

Report mean/std across the five model seeds, without treating seeds or overlapping windows as independent traffic replications. First average each model's counts/outcomes across seeds within each session. Use 2,000 paired session-cluster bootstrap resamples, stratified by attack family and benign condition, and recompute pooled confusion-count metrics for 95% intervals and paired hybrid-minus-baseline differences. Report macro recall across families too. With one long capture, use contiguous blocks longer than the dependence horizon and disclose the assumption; repeated seeds cannot create attack diversity.

When enough independent sessions exist, perform a paired permutation test on session-level differences, with Holm adjustment across the prespecified hybrid-versus-baseline comparisons. Report effect sizes and intervals before p-values. With very few attack episodes, present descriptive intervals and explicit uncertainty instead of a strong significance claim. Threshold sweeps are diagnostic curves after freezing; no test-derived threshold becomes the headline operating point.

title: Methodology component analysis failures and outputs

rows: Whether the detector depends mainly on volume
Low-rate recall compared with volume-only inputs

items: Retrain each applicable variant on the same groups, then recalibrate its complete final rule on the same development benign sets to the same FPR target. Keep seeds and testing fixed. Recalibration is necessary because removing a branch changes the score scale. Also show an optional fixed-threshold removal only as a diagnostic, clearly distinguished from the matched-operating-point comparison.

Inspect false positives by legitimate workload, destination, protocol and session. Inspect false negatives by excluded family, measured rate, active connections, attack duration and client count. Plot benign-stress and attack score overlap; distinguish data/label errors from model errors. Check cold-start misses, alert lag, missing features, exporter timeouts and residual identifier leakage. Examine cases where legitimate congestion and malicious resource exhaustion have similar metadata; if the available features cannot separate them, report the observability limit.

Record whether a missed lab trace actually degraded service. Keep attempted attacks and successful denial-of-service episodes distinguishable. Threshold or feature changes suggested by final-test errors belong to a future iteration requiring a new untouched test set; they are not retroactively applied to improve this study.

Produce the fitted detection pipeline, frozen feature schema, preprocessing parameters, C1 score maps, final decision threshold, model configurations, seeds and an environment file. Release scripts or notebooks for extraction, manifest generation, fitting and evaluation, plus licence-compatible dataset links and hashes. The evaluation report will include matched baseline results, per-family confusion matrices, stress FPR, recall-delay curves, paired uncertainty intervals, ablation tables and labelled failure examples.

The practical output is a timestamped destination-service alert with supervised score, reconstruction score, combined score and persistence state. The scientific output is evidence for or against the hypotheses, including situations where a simple baseline is sufficient or every method fails. No accuracy, novelty or deployment claim will be made until these measurements exist.

items: Public captures may contain few independent slow-attack episodes, correlated flows, schedule-derived labels or data errors. Grouped splits, provenance audits and session-level uncertainty reduce these risks but cannot create attack diversity. An older public dataset and a small lab do not represent all operational traffic. Lab workload generators may make benign stress artificially easy; use several traffic seeds and match load ranges across benign and malicious conditions where feasible.

A false-positive target selected on development benign traffic can drift on a new network. Report transfer failure directly. Destination aggregation may dilute very weak attacks or mix simultaneous families; label ambiguous windows and examine dilution separately. CPU inference speed does not demonstrate IoT-device deployability. The core implementation is CPU-oriented; federated training, large GANs and production response integration are excluded to keep the plan feasible.
